data.text/markdown:
Findings

Formula and fingerprint models distinguish the selected groups well. Predicting actual plant activity still requires verified biological labels. All model comparisons below use 171 compounds (55 herbicides, 116 natural products) and the same five test folds, keeping shared core structures together.

data.text/html:
1. Halogens explain part of the separation

Halogens are much more common in the selected herbicides. Other prominent formula associations involve nitrogen, element count, carbon and oxygen; these are associations within this collection.

2. Fingerprints work; removing halogens weakens the formula model

Recomputing composition without halogens lowers AUROC 0.952 → 0.913. RDKit Morgan logistic/forest models reach 0.947–0.949 AUROC; neither improves balanced accuracy over the original formula model here.AUROC measures ranking; balanced accuracy averages performance on the two groups. These scores predict selection membership, not verified herbicidal activity, benignity or natural origin. Settings are exploratory; no independent biological validation is available.

data.text/markdown:
3. Biological verification is the next step

  • Dietary comparison expanded: 200 verified benign compounds, including all 40 pilot identities (160 additional). All 200 SMILES/key pairs agree; fingerprints are available for all 200 and formula features for
    1. This advances the dietary comparator group; plant inactivity is not established by dietary benignity.
  • Assay review: 154 compounds; 15 full external identity matches and one connectivity-only match. Li 7b / CHEMBL2253255 is on hold: reported allyl and frozen cyclopropyl structures differ.
  • New leads: 5 additional fingerprinted identity candidates; 6 names unresolved. No activity model has been fitted from these additions.
Next: retain the benignity citations/dose limits, reconcile the 16 original selection overlaps, resolve 7b and agree the biological endpoint/group definitions. The herbicide–allelopath–benign comparison remains open.

Verification: exact next actions

Working instructions, separate from the presentation findings above. An editable pack is ready at analysis/outputs/manual-verification-2026-11-05/. The full instructions are in analysis/docs/verification-checklist.md. Original source files remain unchanged; no human decisions have been filled in. New priority: resolve Li 7b / CHEMBL2253255 first. The latest release reports an allyl-versus-cyclopropyl discrepancy; keep activity unknown until original PDF/SI and chemistry review resolve it. Then check 7w and KIH-6127 geometry. See analysis/docs/verification-release.md and the section 6c tables. For the Li/He plant-assay compounds:
  1. Start with assays/li2006_source_mapping.csv (24 rows), then review he2011_source_mapping.csv (58 rows) separately. Obtain each original PDF/SI.
  2. Compare the paper's structure with the matching computed SVG sheet in assays/structure_drawings/. Record the paper compound number, structure page and exact match/unresolved/conflict decision. Get chemistry help if unsure.
  3. Find that compound's exact result row and species/dose/application column. Save a cited excerpt and transcribe the original symbol, grade or inequality.
  4. Record species/stage, rate and units, application mode, duration, controls and replication from the methods. Record missing details and conflicts explicitly.
  5. Agree a source-specific decision rule with the research lead. Record human reviewer/date, the accepted policy and approval reference. Unresolved evidence remains unknown; a low response applies only to the declared assay conditions.
  6. Transfer only accepted decisions into separately versioned seven-column label files, one policy per file. Run analysis/validate_activity_proposal.py with the frozen latest audit (exact command in the release assessment). It checks the new hold as well as schema; passing does not verify scientific approval. Broaden scaffold support before activity modeling.
For the new 200-compound list: retain the verification already performed as linked citations, dose/population/duration limits and reviewer decisions. Check CID correspondence and reconcile overlaps before a new model. Section 6.1 shows the structural audit. The earlier 40-row worksheets below remain useful reference material; their frozen statuses do not describe the newer verification. For the historical 40-compound pilot records:
  1. Use dietary/triage_reference.csv to prioritize review; start with the 12 provisional cases. Edit dietary/review.csv, not the frozen original.
  2. Define a specific population, oral amount/units, duration and endpoint. Match the exact compound/form and document occurrence in the claimed organism.
  3. Read the primary exposure evidence and each flag in context. Record the dose, route/time, restrictions, citation, reviewer and bounded decision. Food use and absence of warnings alone do not establish high-dose safety.
  4. Obtain separate suitable plant-assay evidence before calling any dietary candidate plant-inactive. The four natural-active occurrence leads likewise require their own identity, activity and ecological-role checks.

Supporting analysis and source evidence

The sections below document the methods, model comparisons, errors, dietary triage and deeper assay-review audit behind the presentation findings. Frozen model products passed their saved SHA-256 checks. All eight held-out AUROC/balanced-accuracy pairs were recomputed, shared compound/fold assignments checked and scaffold leakage rejected. The triage and deeper-review sections verify their own saved audit products. This notebook reads evidence; it does not retrieve compounds, fit models, assign labels or edit the working copies.

1. Define exactly what the existing result measures

The evaluation cohort is 55 selected herbicides and 116 selected natural products, after the established identity/formula eligibility and deduplication policy. The prepared selection was larger (176); this diagnostic uses the same complete 171-compound cohort as the older ablations. Source membership=1 means selected herbicide; source membership=0 means selected natural product. Five fixed scaffold-held-out folds keep compounds with the same RDKit scaffold together. The same compounds/folds are used for every profile. Training-only preprocessing avoids exposing the held-out compounds to fitting. No seed/threshold/hyperparameter search was performed; the cutoff remains 0.5. All acyclic chemistry shares the ACYCLIC group under the existing policy. AUROC measures ranking; balanced accuracy averages sensitivity and specificity at the chosen cutoff. They answer different questions. High selection accuracy can reflect how the lists were assembled, rather than herbicidal efficacy.

data.text/html:
2. Test the halogen hypothesis

37/55 selected herbicides have halogens, versus 1/116 natural products. Presence alone reaches 83.21% balanced accuracy, so it is a strong clue. It does not recover all the original performance. Two ablations distinguish direct columns from indirect composition clues: (a) drop F/Cl/Br/I counts and fractions; (b) additionally recalculate element count, atom count and all remaining fractions without halogens. The stricter ablation still reaches 0.9130 AUROC / 82.15% balanced accuracy. This supports additional signal. It does not establish causal elemental effects, or chemically simulate replacing halogens in real molecules.

3. Compare formula and fingerprint classifiers

Morgan fingerprints describe local atom environments up to radius 2 in 2048 binary bits, with chirality included. They use the existing RDKit generator; the first linked paper proposes MAP4, a different fingerprint. MAP4 was not added or benchmarked here. Raw Morgan logistic uses class-balanced L2 logistic regression, C=1, without scaling or PCA. The forest uses 500 trees, minimum leaf size 2, square-root feature sampling and class-balanced weights. These are fixed exploratory baselines. Both reach 88.66% balanced accuracy; their AUROCs are 0.9467 and 0.9487. Neither improves on the original formula result at cutoff 0.5. This does not show fingerprints are generally inferior: cohort, settings, sample size and operating point all matter.

4. Identify which formula features contribute

The raw standardized formula comparator has nearly the same AUROC as the original PCA model. Its strongest mean absolute coefficients are N count, Cl count, element count, C count and O count. Positive means association with selected herbicides; negative means association with natural products. Coefficients are per training-fold standard deviation, under L2 regularization. Held-out permutation checks shuffle each feature ten times per test fold. A joint halogen shuffle keeps relationships inside that block together. Mean AUC drops are approximately 0.0543 (joint halogens), 0.0493 (N count), 0.0304 (Cl count). Negative drops can occur through noise. These explain the raw formula comparator, not the original PCA model. Counts/fractions are correlated: coefficients can be redistributed and individual permutation effects masked. Shuffling can create impossible formulas. Fold ranges and permutation SD are descriptive, not confidence intervals, p-values or causal attribution. Do not sum the drops as variance explained or interpret larger coefficients as biological mechanisms.

5. Inspect the held-out errors

morgan_forest: 13 incorrect classifications at 0.5. Fingerprint logistic and forest each have 43 TP, 12 FN, 115 TN and 1 FP. Scores are selection probabilities under this experiment; they are not calibrated probabilities of toxicity. The errors below are useful review leads, not automatically wrong biological labels.

6. Original 40-compound dietary pilot (historical)

These are the frozen pilot results, before the subsequent 200-compound user verification summarized in section 6.1. The candidate list contains 40 names: 20 amino acids, six sugars, five polyols, seven fatty acids and two organic acids. PubChem supplied the CID, isomeric SMILES and InChIKey; RDKit independently regenerated every InChIKey. All 40 agree, parse successfully and have fingerprints/descriptors. This verifies identity consistency, not correct stereoisomer choice or safety. 37 are pending human review; 3 are on hold; 0 have accepted high-dose or plant-negative labels. Caprylic/capric acids occur in registered herbicide products even though they have edible-source food-use provisions. Lauric acid is held conservatively for biological-activity review. Xylitol has a dog-toxicity warning. Fructose/maltose source provisions concern mixtures; an isolated compound's exposure must be checked separately. The source overlap audit finds L-proline already in the natural-product selection. It cannot be assigned opposite roles or split across folds. 29/40 candidates share ACYCLIC, so this pilot has substantial chemical family bias. More names alone will not create independent chemistry. Dose, population, route/duration and natural-occurrence references remain blank for human review. No candidate was inserted into model training.

6.1. Expanded dietary comparison · 5 November 2026

The new notes/plant_animal_food_compounds_200.tsv contains 200 unique names, CIDs and supplied keys. The user reports these compounds were verified benign. This audit checks the supplied chemical records; the four-column TSV does not include the supporting exposure/reviewer records. Identity and features: all 200 SMILES parse; all computed InChIKeys match; all have Morgan fingerprints. The current formula workflow supports 192; eight charged records are unsupported. CID-to-structure correspondence has not been independently re-fetched. Name/key consistency and benignity evidence are separate checks. What is new: all 40 earlier pilot identities are present, so there are 160 additional full-key identities, not 200 additional controls. The older pilot's automated-review statuses above/below describe its frozen evidence, not a reassessment of the user's subsequent verification. Chemical diversity: 43 scaffold groups; 98/200 compounds share ACYCLIC. Counts of compounds do not equal counts of independent chemical families.Overlap: 16 exact original-selection matches; 17 when including connectivity-only matches. Keep shared identities/families together across splits. No full or connectivity matches occur with the 154 assay candidates. What this enables: a larger herbicide-versus-dietary-comparator experiment, with the benignity claim's population, dose and duration documented. It does not establish plant-inactive controls or a numerical herbicide–allelopath–benign ordering. Preserve the original four columns; retain verification sources, dose limits, reviewer/date and decision in a linked record. Reconcile overlaps and check CIDs before model evaluation. No biological targets were assigned and no new classifier was fitted by this structural audit. All saved target columns remain null.

6a. Automated review of the original 40-compound pilot (historical)

12 provisional dietary candidates · 26 priority review · 2 exclusions from a presumed plant-inactive group. This is a review queue, not a new biological label file. All high-dose and plant-activity labels remain unknown. Provisional list: Glycerol, Glycine, L-Alanine, L-Asparagine, L-Aspartic acid, L-Glutamic acid, L-Isoleucine, L-Leucine, L-Serine, L-Threonine, L-Tyrosine, L-Valine. The process saved 95 requests: 40 PubChem hazard sections, 40 toxicity sections and 15 food-use documents. Ninety-four returned HTTP 200; xylitol's hazard section returned 404. Food checks used 2025 annual CFR XML or FDA GRAS pages. Thirty-eight names have conditional food-use leads; fructose/HFCS and maltose/malt syrup remain mixture-scoped. Verify current conditions, exact compound form and exposure before accepting a comparator. The rules separate GHS handling warnings from systemic codes, known population/dose cautions, prior holds, identity overlaps and family-specific exposure questions. They also scan selected human-toxicity/interaction passages. This promotes tryptophan, methionine, lysine and glutamine out of the simpler 16-candidate pilot shortlist. Eleven candidates have text review hits in the final run. A text hit is not a harmful-effect finding. Matches can describe null results, contamination, co-exposures, historical evidence or other species. GHS reports can vary across suppliers and conditions. Absence of a trigger does not clear the compound; the provisional group merely has fewer flags under this bounded policy. This is not an exhaustive literature review or a validated automated safety classifier. Missingness stays visible: five rows have gaps, even though the standalone evidence-gap category has zero entries (priority flags take precedence). These include unavailable/missing xylitol, lactose and L-malic-acid sections or extracted text, plus the two mixture-scoped food references.

6b. Connecting the deeper compound review · 5 November 2026

It does not add another independent dataset or replace the dietary comparator review. External identities and source-review priorities

Read the comparison/status columns before interpreting a match. Resolve 7b first, then the remaining Li uncertainties and He source mappings.

Additional natural-product leads

Five of the 11 names resolved to single PubChem identity candidates with internally consistent SMILES/keys; their fingerprints are in the separate new_lead_features.parquet. Six 404 name searches remain unresolved, not discarded. Every target remains null. Match original paper/SI structures before accepting identities; assess occurrence and plant response separately. The 2021 primary leaf study reports lesion diameters on punctured/intact detached green-foxtail leaves. Ophiobolin I has weak punctured-leaf response at the highest concentration and no intact-leaf lesions in Table 1; two other congeners have no lesions under the tested conditions. Record dose, leaf treatment and duration before considering bounded low-response labels. Keep mixture synergy and anticancer endpoints separate from individual herbicidal activity. Full file-by-file assessment, sources, reproduction command and hold-aware label-check command: analysis/docs/verification-release.md. These findings supplement the dietary review; they establish neither benign high-dose controls nor the proposed herbicide–allelopath–benign ordering.

7. What would “allelopaths in the middle” mean?

The professor's proposal is a testable hypothesis, not an ordering built into these labels. An allelopath may be a potent herbicide; a human food compound may injure plants. The natural selection also contains response markers, so it is not a fully reviewed set of allelopaths. This descriptive molecular-weight/logP view displays the source selections and new review candidates. The shared proline identity is omitted from the dietary points. This historical projection uses the original 40-compound pilot, not the expanded 200-compound list in section 6.1. It is not an activity axis or a statistical test of a midpoint. Pan/zoom and hover to inspect family/size differences that a future model could exploit. A validated middle-group claim requires independent reviewed labels and a declared score/endpoint/contrast.

data.text/markdown:
8. What you must do before calling this an activity/safety model

  1. Agree the target with your professor. A source-group classifier, a human dietary-safety classifier and a plant-inhibition classifier are three different questions. For plant activity, predeclare species, endpoint, concentration, duration, controls and active/inactive thresholds. Record natural occurrence and non-target hazard separately.
  2. Retain the verification behind the 200 dietary compounds. Link the supplied TSV to primary references, dose/unit, population, route/duration, reviewer/date and exceptions. Confirm CID correspondence and reconcile the 16 exact original-selection overlaps plus the additional connectivity match. The older 40-row worksheet retains useful flags; its frozen statuses are historical. Keep dietary benignity separate from tested plant inactivity. Preserve original inputs and save decisions in a versioned linked record.
  3. Review actual plant assays. Existing frozen ChEMBL material has 157 measurements from 14 assays/publications but no accepted activity labels. Start with analysis/docs/label_review_guide.md; review the original paper and assay methods. Low response in one assay is not universal inactivity. Keep unknown/conflicting outcomes explicit.
  4. Then compare the three groups. Obtain diverse reviewed herbicides, allelopaths and suitable comparators, reserve independent chemistry and publications, deduplicate overlaps, and evaluate formula and fingerprint logistic/forest models using matching holdouts. A three-class classifier has no inherent ordinal “middle”; alternatively train a declared binary contrast and assess an independent allelopath score distribution.
  5. Validate before screening. Report AUROC, balanced accuracy, confusion, precision–recall, calibration and similarity/domain limits. Keep an independent test set out of profile/threshold choices. Confirm efficacy and non-target hazard separately before proposing safer bioherbicides.
What you can tell your professor now: “The halogen hypothesis is supported (37/55 versus 1/116), but non-halogen composition also separates the selection. I reproduced the formula result and tested raw Morgan logistic and forest models on the same scaffold folds. The dietary comparison now has 200 compounds reported verified benign; all supplied SMILES/key pairs agree, with 160 identities beyond the pilot. Dietary benignity does not establish plant inactivity. Actual activity prediction and the three-group ordering still depend on reviewed biological labels.”

Reproduce and inspect the evidence

From the repository root: 
UV_CACHE_DIR=analysis/.uv-cache uv run --project analysis marimo run notes/notebooks/findings.py
Use edit instead of run to change the notebook. A static export is at notes/notebooks/findings.html; selectors need the live notebook. Implementation/reproduction commands and input/output contracts are in analysis/docs/diagnostics-review.md (professor follow-up) and analysis/docs/compound_sources.md (dietary pilot). Dated scientific results are in analysis/FINDINGS.md. Research outputs/raw snapshots remain local and ignored; the requested notebook is selectively committed under notes. Output hashes verify integrity, not scientific validity. Historical manifests are preserved and current code may evolve separately. Professor's reading list and primary source checks (4 November 2026):
  • MAP4 paper: proposes a different fingerprint combining circular environments with atom-pair distances. It is an alternative to benchmark later, not a prerequisite for the RDKit Morgan baseline.
  • Fingerprint review / PubMed (publisher): overview of fingerprint concepts/applications. Publisher access was restricted; no claim of a full-text implementation from that paper.
  • RDKit fingerprint generator tutorial: generator configuration and bit-environment explanations.
  • Amino-acid food-use conditions, edible-source fatty-acid conditions, EPA herbicide-active table, FDA xylitol warning. Food-use provisions do not establish plant inactivity.
